text: The Filter transformation works exactly like a SQL WHERE clause, built entirely visually. It evaluates one boolean expression per row, and only rows where that expression comes back true actually continue downstream — the same expression language Chapter 4's Lesson 22 already taught you.

The Select transformation reshapes a stream's column list, without ever touching a single row's actual values. Rename a column, drop one entirely, or reorder the output — it's the tool you reach for after a Join brings in duplicate-named columns from both sides, and you genuinely need a clean, deliberate column list before the data reaches a sink.

Derived Column generates brand-new columns, or overwrites existing ones, using a real expression. Type a new name to create a column; select an existing one from the dropdown instead to overwrite it. A genuine real example: a text Rating column gets overwritten with toInteger of Rating — same column name, a completely different, now-numeric type underneath.

When a schema isn't explicitly fixed, or you need to update an entire set of columns at once, a column pattern matches columns by metadata rules and applies that same derived logic to every single match — one rule, applied automatically, however many columns actually match now or as the schema keeps drifting. Next: Join and Aggregate — combining streams together, and collapsing rows into genuinely summarized ones.
